          # '##[' becomes '#?[', so the value can neither end the line nor open
          # the runner's older '##[command]' syntax in the middle of one.
          shown() { local v="${1//[[:cntrl:]]/?}"; printf '%s' "${v//\#\#\[/#?[}"; }
          # Encode, then wrap, for the step summary (#506): a control character
          # becomes a question mark and an ASCII punctuation character its
          # numeric HTML entity (`@` also gets an empty comment after it, so no
          # e-mail autolink forms), inside <code> (md_code) or <pre> (md_pre,
          # line ends kept). Caller and repository text then renders as
          # text and links nothing.
          md_enc() { local LC_ALL=C; local s="${1//[[:cntrl:]]/?}" c n x; s="${s//$'\xc2'[$'\x80'-$'\x9f']/?}"; s="${s//$'\xe2\x80'[$'\xa8\xa9']/?}"; for n in {33..47} {58..64} {91..96} {123..126}; do printf -v x '%x' "$n"; printf -v c '%b' "\\x$x"; s=${s//"$c"/$'\x01'$n$'\x02'}; done; s=${s//$'\x01'64$'\x02'/$'\x01'64$'\x02\x03'}; s=${s//$'\x01'/'&#'}; s=${s//$'\x02'/';'}; s=${s//$'\x03'/'<!-- -->'}; printf '%s' "$s"; }
          md_code() { printf '<code>%s</code>' "$(md_enc "$1")"; }
          md_pre() { local line; printf '<pre>'; while IFS= read -r line; do md_enc "${line%$'\r'}"; printf '\n'; done <<< "$1"; printf '</pre>\n'; }

          # Fail loudly rather than defaulting. An empty ref is what made the
          # old behaviour wrong-but-green for every release so far.
          if [ -z "${FROM_REF}" ]; then
            echo "::error::from_branch resolved to an empty value. On a release" \
                 "trigger it defaults to github.event.release.tag_name; on a" \
                 "manual run, pass the tag explicitly." >&2
            exit 1
          fi

          git fetch --force --tags --prune origin

          # Accept a tag, a branch or a raw SHA, in that order of preference.
          SOURCE_SHA="$(
            git rev-parse --verify --quiet "refs/tags/${FROM_REF}^{commit}" ||
            git rev-parse --verify --quiet "refs/remotes/origin/${FROM_REF}^{commit}" ||
            git rev-parse --verify --quiet "${FROM_REF}^{commit}"
          )" || {
            # from_branch is caller input or a release tag name; masked like
            # the target (#492).
            echo "::error::Could not resolve '$(shown "$FROM_REF")' to a commit." >&2
            exit 1
          }

          EXPECTED="$(git ls-remote origin "refs/heads/${TARGET}" | awk '{print $1}')"

          if [ -z "${EXPECTED}" ]; then
            echo "Target branch '$(shown "$TARGET")' does not exist yet; creating it."
            git push origin "${SOURCE_SHA}:refs/heads/${TARGET}"
            action="created"
          elif [ "${EXPECTED}" = "${SOURCE_SHA}" ]; then
            echo "Target branch '$(shown "$TARGET")' already points at ${SOURCE_SHA}; nothing to do."
            action="already current"
          elif [ "${MODE}" = "merge" ]; then
            # The /merges API, the mechanism that worked before #404 and still
            # works wherever merge commits are allowed. It is additive, so the
            # target keeps whatever it already carries.
            if ! out=$(gh api "repos/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY}/merges" \
                         -f base="${TARGET}" -f head="${SOURCE_SHA}" \
                         -f commit_message="chore(release): refresh ${TARGET} to ${FROM_REF}" 2>&1); then
              # The response is API text and the refs are caller input; all
              # three are masked (#492).
              echo "::error::Merging $(shown "$FROM_REF") into '$(shown "$TARGET")' failed even though the target reports that merge commits are permitted. The protection may have changed since the check, or the token may lack write access. Response: $(shown "$out")" >&2
              exit 1
            fi
            action="merged"
          else
            # --force-with-lease, not --force: if another run advanced the
            # target between the read above and this push, the push aborts
            # instead of discarding that run's work. The concurrency group on
            # this workflow makes that unlikely; the lease makes it safe.
            git push --force-with-lease="${TARGET}:${EXPECTED}" \
              origin "${SOURCE_SHA}:refs/heads/${TARGET}"
            action="reset"
          fi

          previous="${EXPECTED:-<branch did not exist>}"
          {
            echo "### Presentation branch refreshed"
            echo
            echo "| Field | Value |"
            echo "|---|---|"
            echo "| Strategy | $(md_code "$MODE") (${action}) |"
            echo "| Source ref | $(md_code "$FROM_REF") |"
            echo "| Source commit | $(md_code "$SOURCE_SHA") |"
            echo "| Target branch | $(md_code "$TARGET") |"
            echo "| Previous target commit | $(md_code "$previous") |"
          } >> "${GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY}"

      # Failing loudly is the point. The cascade previously left a stale
      # presentation branch behind a green release, which is how v2.0.0 went
      # unnoticed for six weeks. A target this workflow cannot write to is a
      # configuration decision the operator has to make, not something to
      # paper over.
      - name: "Refuse: no permitted write path"
        if: steps.strategy.outputs.mode == 'blocked'
        env:
          TARGET: ${{ inputs.target_branch }}
          FROM_REF: ${{ inputs.from_branch }}
          REASON: ${{ steps.strategy.outputs.reason }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          # Masks $1 for a log line (#492): control characters become '?' and
          # '##[' becomes '#?[', so the value can neither end the line nor open
          # the runner's older '##[command]' syntax in the middle of one.
          shown() { local v="${1//[[:cntrl:]]/?}"; printf '%s' "${v//\#\#\[/#?[}"; }
          # Encode, then wrap, for the step summary (#506): a control character
          # becomes a question mark and an ASCII punctuation character its
          # numeric HTML entity (`@` also gets an empty comment after it, so no
          # e-mail autolink forms), inside <code> (md_code) or <pre> (md_pre,
          # line ends kept). Caller and repository text then renders as
          # text and links nothing.
          md_enc() { local LC_ALL=C; local s="${1//[[:cntrl:]]/?}" c n x; s="${s//$'\xc2'[$'\x80'-$'\x9f']/?}"; s="${s//$'\xe2\x80'[$'\xa8\xa9']/?}"; for n in {33..47} {58..64} {91..96} {123..126}; do printf -v x '%x' "$n"; printf -v c '%b' "\\x$x"; s=${s//"$c"/$'\x01'$n$'\x02'}; done; s=${s//$'\x01'64$'\x02'/$'\x01'64$'\x02\x03'}; s=${s//$'\x01'/'&#'}; s=${s//$'\x02'/';'}; s=${s//$'\x03'/'<!-- -->'}; printf '%s' "$s"; }
          md_code() { printf '<code>%s</code>' "$(md_enc "$1")"; }
          md_pre() { local line; printf '<pre>'; while IFS= read -r line; do md_enc "${line%$'\r'}"; printf '\n'; done <<< "$1"; printf '</pre>\n'; }
          msg="Cannot refresh '${TARGET}' to ${FROM_REF}: ${REASON}. Grant the release App a bypass actor on the target's ruleset, relax the rule, or stop refreshing this branch and point consumers at the release tag instead (issue #414, ADR-001)."
          # msg quotes the caller's target_branch and from_branch; masked so
          # neither can start a workflow command on a new line (#492).
          echo "::error::$(shown "$msg")" >&2
          # The summary repeats msg with both refs encoded (#506); REASON is
          # one of the strategy step's literals and keeps its Markdown.
          {
            echo "### Presentation branch NOT refreshed"
            echo
            echo "Cannot refresh $(md_code "$TARGET") to $(md_code "$FROM_REF"): ${REASON}. Grant the release App a bypass actor on the target's ruleset, relax the rule, or stop refreshing this branch and point consumers at the release tag instead (issue #414, ADR-001)."
            echo
            echo "| Field | Value |"
            echo "|---|---|"
            echo "| Target branch | $(md_code "$TARGET") |"
            echo "| Source ref | $(md_code "$FROM_REF") |"
            echo "| Reason | ${REASON} |"
          } >> "${GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY}"
          exit 1

---
# Portfolio-wide release-drafter commons. Every repository extends this via
# `_extends: gh-plumbing:.github/commons-release-drafter.yml`, so a change here
# reaches the whole portfolio on the next Probot sync.

# $RESOLVED_VERSION, not $NEXT_PATCH_VERSION. Before the resolver below existed
# every release was a patch regardless of what landed, so a `breaking-change`
# label had no effect on the version. That combination is worse than it sounds:
# consumers pin by tag and update through Renovate, and a patch bump is the
# update class most likely to be automerged or waved through -- so the change
# least likely to be scrutinised was the one carrying the break.
name-template: v$RESOLVED_VERSION
tag-template: v$RESOLVED_VERSION

version-resolver:
  major:
    labels:
      - breaking-change
  minor:
    labels:
      - feat
      - enhancement
  # Type labels only. `documentation`, `project-config` and `cicd` used to sit
  # here too; they are area labels boring-cyborg derives from the touched paths
  # (see the Maintenance note below). With `default: patch` they never changed
  # the result, but listing them kept the area/type confusion alive (#475).
  patch:
    labels:
      - fix
      - bug
      - chore
      - docs
      - dependencies
      - security
  default: patch

branches:
  - master
  - develop

# The label lists carry both the Conventional-Commits labels the portfolio
# actually applies (`feat`, `fix`) and the GitHub defaults (`enhancement`,
# `bug`). Previously the categories matched only the defaults, so a PR labelled
# `fix` -- the portfolio convention -- fell into the uncategorised remainder of
# the changelog and never appeared under a heading.
categories:
  - title: 🚀 Features
    labels:
      - "feat"
      - "enhancement"
  - title: 🐛 Bug Fixes
    labels:
      - "fix"
      - "bug"
  # Only labels that are a category in their own right. `project-config`,
  # `cicd` and `dependencies` used to sit here too, and they are *area* labels
  # -- boring-cyborg derives them from the touched paths, so they co-occur with
  # a type label rather than replacing it. release-drafter lists a pull request
  # under every matching category, so `fix(workflows):` appeared under both Bug
  # Fixes and Maintenance, and `fix(vale):` under three headings at once (#413).
  # `documentation` stayed behind and is the same class: boring-cyborg applies
  # it to every pull request touching `docs/**`, so a `fix(ci):` that also
  # updated a page rendered under both Bug Fixes and Maintenance (#475). The
  # type label for a docs pull request is `docs`, from the `docs(...)` title.
  # `.github/scripts/check-release-category-labels.py` refuses the class.
  - title: 🧰 Maintenance
    labels:
      - "chore"
      - "docs"

autolabeler:
  # Derive the type label from the title, so every pull request carries exactly
  # one and the categories above always find it. Without this the type label was
  # applied by hand and the result was arbitrary: of twelve consecutive merges,
  # #415 carried `fix` *and* `chore` (two categories), #418 was a `feat(...)`
  # carrying only `chore` (filed under Maintenance), and #420 carried no type
  # label at all (the uncategorised remainder). Deriving it removes all three
  # shapes at once, and is what makes reducing Maintenance above safe: a pull
  # request touching only `.github/workflows/**` still lands under its type.
  #
  # release-drafter evaluates this block only on `pull_request` and
  # `pull_request_target` events, never on the `push` that updates the draft.
  # A repository gets it by calling `reusable-release-drafter-autolabel.yml`
  # from a `pull_request_target` workflow; without that caller the block is
  # inert and type labels depend on someone applying them by hand -- which is
  # how the fork pull request #461 landed uncategorised (#475).
  #
  # `chore(release):` matches both this and the `release` rule below; that is
  # intended, since `release` is an exclude-label and wins by removing the entry
  # from the notes entirely.
  - label: "feat"
    title:
      - '/^feat(\(.+\))?!?:/'
  - label: "fix"
    title:
      - '/^fix(\(.+\))?!?:/'
  - label: "chore"
    title:
      - '/^chore(\(.+\))?!?:/'
  - label: "docs"
    title:
      - '/^docs(\(.+\))?!?:/'
  - label: "release"
    title:
      - '/^chore\(release\):/'
  # Exploratory work is not something a consumer shipped, so it does not belong
  # in the changelog. Without this pairing an `exp/` pull request landed
  # uncategorised in the "shipped" section, which reads as a delivered change.
  - label: "experimental"
    branch:
      - '/^exp\//'

exclude-labels:
  - "release"
  - "experimental"

# Release notes lint PR titles as metadata, not as prose. A title such as
# `fix(ci): update actionlint and reviewdog` otherwise triggers Vale's spelling
# and terminology rules and blocks publishing. Escape literal backticks so a
# title cannot terminate the inline code span.
# `@$AUTHOR`, not `$AUTHORS`: the reusable pins release-drafter v6.4.0, and
# `$AUTHORS` only exists from v7.6.0 on -- v6 leaves it in the notes verbatim.
# Switch to `$AUTHORS` (co-authors included) together with the v7 bump.
change-template: '- `$TITLE` (#$NUMBER) @$AUTHOR'
change-title-escapes: '`'

template: |
  ## Changes

  $CHANGES

docs.title: Statische Tests
docs.text:
Führt ein minimales Bündel statischer Analyse bei jedem Pull-Request und bei jedem Push auf den Default-Branch aus und liefert schnelles Feedback ohne externe Dienste.

  • pre-commit, in einer festgelegten Version installiert, führt die in .pre-commit-config.yaml definierten Hooks auf allen Dateien aus; actions/cache, auf einen vollständigen Commit-SHA gepinnt, cacht die Hook-Umgebungen (siehe Cache der Hook-Umgebungen)

docs.title: Verwendung
docs.text:
.github/workflows/build-static-tests.yaml
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [develop] # durch den eigenen Default-Branch ersetzen

jobs:
  static:
    uses: nolte/gh-plumbing/.github/workflows/reusable-pre-commit.yaml@<tag>

Erforderlicher Status-Check

Kombiniere den Workflow mit einer Branch-Protection-Regel, die den Check static / Static CI Tests verlangt — siehe Settings.

Fork-Pull-Requests brauchen den Trigger pull_request

Ein Fork pusht nie in das Basis-Repository. Mit einem reinen Push-Trigger meldet sich der erforderliche Check bei einem Pull-Request aus einem Fork nie, und dieser Pull-Request bleibt blockiert. pull_request_target ist keine Alternative. Standardmäßig checkt es den Basis-Branch aus, der erforderliche Check wird also grün, ohne die Änderungen des Pull-Requests zu testen. Checkt man stattdessen den Head des Pull-Requests aus, läuft der Code des Forks mit dem Schreib-Token und den Secrets des Basis-Repositorys. Bei einem Fork-Pull-Request überspringt reusable-trivy.yaml den Upload seines Scan-Berichts in den Security-Tab, weil das Token dort nur Leserechte hat.

docs.title: Fork-Wächter
docs.text:
Erforderliche Checks wie static / Static CI Tests laufen bei pull_request, und GitHub führt einen pull_request-Workflow aus dem Merge-Commit des Pull-Requests aus. Bei einem Fork-Pull-Request stammen die Workflow-Dateien und die Skripte, die sie aufrufen, aus dem Fork. Ein Fork kann sie also so lange ändern, bis jeder Job durchläuft. Ein erforderlicher Kontext nennt nur die App und den Check, daher erfüllt ihn auch ein Check, den der Fork definiert.

reusable-fork-guard.yaml ist der Check, den ein Fork nicht umschreiben kann. Rufe ihn aus einem pull_request_target-Workflow auf und verlange seinen Kontext neben den anderen:

.github/workflows/fork-guard.yaml
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, edited]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  fork-guard:
    permissions:
      contents: read
      statuses: write
    uses: nolte/gh-plumbing/.github/workflows/reusable-fork-guard.yaml@<tag>

Der Workflow meldet sein Ergebnis als Commit-Status fork-guard, und diesen Status verlangst du als Kontext. Der Check schlägt fehl, wenn der Pull-Request aus einem Fork stammt und einen geschützten Pfad hinzufügt, ändert, entfernt oder umbenennt. Standardmäßig sind das .github/*, scripts/*, actions/*, das Taskfile und taskfiles/*, .pre-commit-config.yaml, jede requirements*.txt, die Konfigurationsdateien von pytest und coverage sowie mkdocs.yml. Mit protected-paths ersetzt du die Liste. Jede Zeile ist ein Bash-Muster, und * passt auch auf /. Ein Pull-Request aus einem Branch desselben Repositorys besteht den Check. Um eine berechtigte Fork-Änderung an einem geschützten Pfad zu übernehmen, pusht ein Maintainer sie erneut auf einen Branch des Repositorys.

Warum pull_request_target hier sicher ist

pull_request_target führt die Definition aus dem Default-Branch aus, der Pull-Request kann also weder den Check noch seine Liste ändern. Der Workflow checkt nichts aus und liest keinen Dateiinhalt. Er listet die geänderten Dateinamen über die Compare-API und vergleicht sie als reine Zeichenketten. Sein einziges Schreibrecht ist statuses, um das Ergebnis zu melden. Füge ihm keinen Checkout hinzu.

Den Status verlangen, nicht den Check-Run

Der Check-Run des Jobs heißt fork-guard / Protected Paths. Verlange diesen Namen nicht: Ein Fork kann einen Workflow mit einem gleichnamigen Job hinzufügen, der durchläuft, und dieselbe App meldet dann beide Check-Runs. Einen Commit-Status kann ein Fork nicht setzen, weil das Token seines pull_request-Laufs nur Leserechte hat.

Den Kontext einführen

pull_request_target führt die Workflow-Datei aus dem Basis-Branch aus. Merge den Workflow vor oder zusammen mit der Änderung, die seinen Kontext verlangt. Die Branch-Protection ändert sich erst, wenn die Settings den Default-Branch erreichen, und dann liegt der Workflow schon dort.

docs.title: Cache der Hook-Umgebungen
docs.text:
Der Workflow cacht ~/.cache/pre-commit, wo pre-commit die Hook-Umgebungen installiert. Der Cache-Key setzt sich aus dem Betriebssystem-Release des Runners, der installierten pre-commit-Version, dem Python-Installationspfad und einem Hash der .pre-commit-config.yaml zusammen. Ein neues Ubuntu-Image hinter ubuntu-latest oder eine neue pre-commit-Version startet deshalb einen frischen Cache, statt Umgebungen wiederherzustellen, die für ein anderes System gebaut wurden.

Wiederherstellen und Speichern sind getrennte Schritte. Der Workflow speichert den Cache nur in einem pull_request-Lauf, nur bei einem Cache-Miss und bevor pre-commit run irgendeinen Hook ausführt. Einen Cache, den ein Pull-Request-Lauf speichert, sieht nur dieser Pull-Request. Läufe auf dem Default-Branch, Pushes auf andere Branches und pull_request_target-Läufe stellen höchstens wieder her und speichern nie. So kann Hook-Code keine Hook-Umgebungen in den Cache des Default-Branches schreiben, aus dem jeder Branch des Repositorys wiederherstellt.

Weniger Cache-Treffer

Der Default-Branch erhält nie einen gespeicherten Cache. Läufe auf dem Default-Branch und der erste Lauf jedes Pull-Requests installieren die Hook-Umgebungen von Grund auf, der nächste Lauf desselben Pull-Requests stellt sie wieder her. Ein Aufrufer, der den Workflow nur bei push auslöst, nutzt den Cache nie.

Restrisiko

Hook-Code läuft auf dem Runner und kann das Token lesen, mit dem der Runner den Cache-Dienst anspricht. Damit kann Hook-Code weiterhin jeden Cache-Eintrag im Scope des aktuellen Laufs schreiben, auf dem Default-Branch also im Scope des Default-Branches. Die Trennung von Wiederherstellen und Speichern schließt diesen Weg nicht. Das gelingt nur, wenn die Hooks isoliert vom Runner laufen, zum Beispiel in einem Container ohne den Runner-Kontext.

docs.title: Docker-Hub-Rate-Limits
docs.text:
Ein Hook mit language: docker_image zieht sein Image bei jedem Lauf, und pre-commit kann es nicht cachen: Diese Sprache setzt ENVIRONMENT_DIR = None mit install_environment = no_install, das Image bleibt also im Store des Docker-Daemons und landet nie unter ~/.cache/pre-commit — dem einzigen Pfad, den dieser Workflow an actions/cache übergibt.

Ein anonymer Pull zählt gegen ein Budget, das an der Quell-IP hängt, und GitHub-gehostete Runner teilen sich ihre Ausgangsadressen plattformweit. Die Lane verbraucht damit ein Budget, das jedes andere Repository im selben Runner-Netz ebenfalls verbraucht — eine Rate-Limit-Ablehnung kann einen erforderlichen Check also aus einem Grund rot färben, der nichts mit dem Diff zu tun hat.

Zwei optionale Parameter verschieben die Zählung auf ein Konto-Budget:

Parameter Art Default Zweck dockerhub-username Input "" Docker-Hub-Kontoname. Ein Benutzername ist nicht geheim, deshalb reist er als Input. Leer überspringt den Login-Schritt. dockerhub-token Secret nicht gesetzt Docker-Hub-Personal-Access-Token zu diesem Konto. Es muss den Scope „Public Repo Read-only“ haben, weil pre-commit-Hooks im selben Job es lesen können.

Das Token gehört zu einer eigenen Docker ID, die nur die CI nutzt (ein Bot-Konto), nicht zu einer persönlichen, und bekommt ein Ablaufdatum und regelmäßige Rotation. Da Hook-Code es lesen kann, verbraucht ein Leck dann nur das Pull-Kontingent dieses Kontos und legt keine anderswo genutzte Identität offen. Aus demselben Grund persistiert der Workflow das Checkout-Token nicht (persist-credentials: false). Ein Hook, der von origin fetcht, funktioniert deshalb nur in einem öffentlichen Repository, und ein privater Aufrufer braucht einen eigenen Workflow.

.github/workflows/build-static-tests.yaml
jobs:
  static:
    uses: nolte/gh-plumbing/.github/workflows/reusable-pre-commit.yaml@<tag>
    with:
      dockerhub-username: ${{ vars.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
    secrets:
      dockerhub-token: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

Beide Parameter sind optional

Ein Aufrufer, der keinen von beiden übergibt, läuft exakt so wie vor ihrer Einführung: Der Login-Schritt wird übersprungen, die Pulls bleiben anonym. Ein Repository, dessen .pre-commit-config.yaml keinen language: docker_image-Hook deklariert, gewinnt nichts durch das Setzen.

Ein defektes Credential degradiert, es lässt den Lauf nicht scheitern

Der Login-Schritt trägt continue-on-error. Ein abgelaufenes Token, ein Token, das einem Fork-Pull-Request vorenthalten wird, oder ein Benutzername ohne Token fallen alle auf anonyme Pulls zurück und erzeugen eine Warning-Annotation. Hart zu scheitern würde die erforderliche Lane bei jedem Pull-Request rot färben — schlimmer als das Rate-Limit, das der Login vermeidet. Das Run-Log nennt immer den verwendeten Modus.

Warum kein GHCR-Mirror?

Die Hooks auf einen Mirror zu zeigen, braucht ein entry:-Override und entkoppelt damit den Image-Tag vom rev: des Hooks. Genau dieses rev: beobachtet die Update-Automatisierung — der Mirror würde unbeobachtet altern.

docs.title: Shell-Lint
docs.text:
reusable-shellcheck.yaml prüft Shell-Skripte mit ShellCheck. Der Workflow installiert ein festgelegtes ShellCheck-Release und prüft dessen Prüfsumme, bevor er es ausführt; die Version ändert sich also nur mit einem Release dieses Repositorys. Er prüft jede passende Datei, nicht nur die in einem Pull-Request geänderten, und meldet jeden Befund als Annotation: als Fehler, als Warnung oder, für die Stufen info und style, als Hinweis. Er braucht nur contents: read und schreibt nichts in den Pull-Request.

.github/workflows/build-static-tests.yaml
jobs:
  shellcheck:
    permissions:
      contents: read
    uses: nolte/gh-plumbing/.github/workflows/reusable-shellcheck.yaml@<tag>
Input Standard Zweck fail_level error Schweregrad, ab dem der Job fehlschlägt: error, warning, info, any oder none. Befunde darunter annotiert der Job, ohne fehlzuschlagen. path . Basisverzeichnis der Suche, eines pro Zeile. Ein Pfad, den es nicht gibt, lässt den Job fehlschlagen. pattern *.sh Dateinamensmuster der Skripte, eines pro Zeile. exclude */.git/* Pfadmuster, das ausgelassen wird, eines pro Zeile. Ein Wert ersetzt den Standard. check_all_files_with_shebangs false Prüft zusätzlich jede Datei, deren erste Zeile sh, bash, dash oder ksh als Interpreter nennt, unabhängig vom Dateinamen. shellcheck_flags --external-sources Flags für ShellCheck, an Leerzeichen und Zeilenenden getrennt. Das Ausgabeformat setzt der Workflow selbst.

Der Job ist grün, wenn keine Datei passt. Ein Repository ohne Shell-Skripte kann den Workflow daher schon aufrufen, bevor es welche hat.

Der Workflow liefert kein Artefakt, derselbe Aufruf funktioniert also als Gate in einem Release-Pfad. Mit needs: vor den veröffentlichenden Job gesetzt, stoppt ein Befund ab fail_level die Veröffentlichung:

.github/workflows/release-publish.yml
jobs:
  shellcheck:
    permissions:
      contents: read
    uses: nolte/gh-plumbing/.github/workflows/reusable-shellcheck.yaml@<tag>
  publish:
    needs: shellcheck
    permissions:
      contents: write
    uses: nolte/gh-plumbing/.github/workflows/reusable-release-publish.yml@<tag>

Skripte in Workflow-Dateien

Der Workflow liest nur Skriptdateien. Die Shell in den run:-Blöcken von Workflow-Dateien deckt reusable-actionlint.yaml ab.

.github/workflows/reusable-pre-commit.yaml
name: Reusable — Pre-Commit

# Runs the consumer's `.pre-commit-config.yaml`. Most consumers put this job
# behind the `static / Static CI Tests` required check, so anything that can
# redden it for a reason unrelated to the diff is a defect in this file, not in
# the pull request that happens to be unlucky.
#
# One such reason is Docker Hub rate limiting. A hook declared with
# `language: docker_image` pulls its image on every run, and pre-commit cannot
# cache it -- `pre_commit/languages/docker_image.py` sets `ENVIRONMENT_DIR = None`
# with `install_environment = no_install`, so the image lives only in the Docker
# daemon's store and never lands under `~/.cache/pre-commit`, which is the only
# path this workflow hands to `actions/cache`. There is nothing for that cache
# to hold. Measured on nolte/kamerplanter#1321, whose two hooks
# (`rhysd/actionlint`, `koalaman/shellcheck-precommit`) return
# `ratelimit-limit: 100;w=3600` with no publisher exemption.
#
# The decisive property of an anonymous pull is not the number but the bucket:
# it is counted per source IP, and GitHub-hosted runners share egress addresses
# across the whole platform. So the budget this lane spends is shared with every
# other repository that happens to land on the same runner network, and no
# amount of restraint here protects it. Authenticating moves the count to a
# per-account bucket that only this organization draws on.
#
# `docker/login-action` writes `~/.docker/config.json` on the runner, and
# pre-commit's docker_image language shells out to `docker run` against the same
# host daemon (`pre_commit/languages/docker.py:docker_cmd`), so the credentials
# apply to the hook pulls without either side knowing about the other.
#
# Deliberately NOT done: mirroring the images to GHCR and pointing the hooks at
# the mirror through an `entry:` override. That decouples the image tag from the
# hook's `rev:`, which is the pin Renovate actually watches; the mirror would
# then age unwatched. See nolte/kamerplanter#1321.
#
# Deliberately NOT done: pre-pulling the images and shuttling them through
# `actions/cache` with `docker save`/`docker load`. It needs no credentials,
# which is genuinely attractive for a shared reusable, but a consumer's
# `.pre-commit-config.yaml` names only `repo:`/`rev:`/`id:` -- the image
# reference lives in the *hook* repository's `.pre-commit-hooks.yaml`, so this
# workflow would have to clone every hook repo at its `rev` to learn what to
# pull, duplicating what `pre-commit install-hooks` already does. And on a cache
# miss (a `rev` bump, a 7-day eviction, a feature branch that cannot read
# another branch's cache) the pull is anonymous again, so it lowers the
# frequency of the failure without removing it. Authentication removes it.

on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      dockerhub-username:
        description: |
          Docker Hub account name used to authenticate the image pulls made by
          `language: docker_image` pre-commit hooks. A username is not secret --
          it appears in every image reference -- so it travels as an input, and
          only its token half travels as a secret. This mirrors the
          `app-id` input / `app-private-key` secret split in
          `reusable-branch-protection-audit.yaml`, and it is also what makes the
          gate expressible: the `secrets` context is not available in a step's
          `if:`, so a secret alone cannot decide whether a step runs.

          OPTIONAL. Empty -- the default, and what every consumer that has not
          changed its call gets -- skips the login step and pulls anonymously,
          which is exactly the behaviour this workflow had before the input
          existed. Consumers whose `.pre-commit-config.yaml` declares no
          `language: docker_image` hook have nothing to gain by setting it.
        required: false
        type: string
        default: ""
    secrets:
      dockerhub-token:
        description: |
          Docker Hub personal access token matching `inputs.dockerhub-username`.
          It MUST be created with the "Public Repo Read-only" access scope.
          Nothing in this workflow pushes, and a wider scope is not merely
          unnecessary but exposed: the hook environments are installed before
          the login, but the hooks that `pre-commit run` then executes in every
          non-docker language (e.g. python, node, golang, system, script) run on
          the host in the same job and can read `~/.docker/config.json` while
          they run. The post-step logout of `docker/login-action` does not
          revoke a token that was already read, and with passwordless sudo a
          hook can also read it from runner memory. The scope is therefore the
          only control: anything broader than public read-only would be handed
          to third-party hook code. Required in practice whenever
          `dockerhub-username` is set, but declared optional so that a caller
          which sets neither still resolves.
        required: false

# Explicit permissions per spec/project/github-actions-best-practices §B:
# workflow level is the minimum, write scopes are granted per job.
permissions:
  contents: read # checkout + pre-commit; the hooks never push


jobs:
  static:
    name: "Static CI Tests"
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout sources
        uses: actions/checkout@d23441a48e516b6c34aea4fa41551a30e30af803 # v6.1.0
        with:
          # Not persisted, like the consumer checkout in
          # `reusable-docs-freshness.yaml` (the remaining checkouts follow in
          # #471). `pre-commit run` executes hook code from third-party
          # repositories later in this job, and a persisted token -- in v6 a
          # file under `$RUNNER_TEMP` that `.git/config` includes -- is
          # readable by any process in the job.
          # This removes the unprivileged path, a file any process can read; it
          # is not a boundary against hostile hook code. Hooks run with
          # passwordless sudo on GitHub-hosted runners and can read the runner
          # process's memory, so the real limit on the job token is
          # `permissions: contents: read`.
          # Nothing here needs authenticated git: the job holds `contents: read`
          # only, and pre-commit clones the hook repositories into its own cache
          # anonymously. A future private consumer whose hook fetches `origin`
          # would need a workflow of its own rather than a token left lying here.
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-python@ece7cb06caefa5fff74198d8649806c4678c61a1 # v6.3.0
        with:
          # Concrete rather than '3.x', matching the other reusables and
          # .tool-versions. This workflow sits behind `static / Static CI Tests`,
          # which is the one required check most consumers enforce, so a
          # floating interpreter here can turn a green pipeline red with no
          # commit behind it. #400 pinned the input defaults elsewhere and
          # missed this hardcoded one.
          python-version: '3.14'

      # The install, freeze and cache steps below and `Run pre-commit` at the
      # end replace `pre-commit/action` v3.0.1, a composite action whose own
      # cache step references `actions/cache@v4` by tag. The repository setting
      # `sha_pinning_required` checks nested references as well, so a single
      # tag two levels down fails the whole job. Inlining the composite puts
      # every `uses:` under this file's control, where it is pinned to a full
      # commit SHA. The hook-environment install and the Docker Hub login sit
      # between the cache restore and the run; see `Install hook environments`.
      - name: Install pre-commit
        # Inline rather than `-r requirements-dev.txt`: this reusable runs in
        # the consumer's checkout, where no gh-plumbing requirements file
        # exists. Same version as `requirements-dev.txt`: the preset's inline
        # pip pin manager tracks this line, and its `pre-commit` group bumps
        # both pins on one branch (#467).
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          python -m pip install pre-commit==4.7.0

      - name: List installed Python packages
        # Kept from the composite action, so the log still records the exact
        # resolved versions consumers have been able to read there.
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          python -m pip freeze --local

      - name: Compute the hook-environment cache key
        id: cache-key
        # The hook environments hold binaries built against the runner's system
        # libraries (wheels, nodeenv) and are laid out by one pre-commit
        # version, so the key carries both (#468). `pythonLocation` alone does
        # not move when `ubuntu-latest` switches to a new Ubuntu release. The
        # pre-commit version is read from the installed package rather than
        # repeated here, so the key follows the pin above without a second
        # copy of it. The `pre-commit-4` prefix retires every key built under
        # `pre-commit/action`'s `pre-commit-3` layout; consumers take one cold
        # cache, once.
        env:
          CONFIG_HASH: ${{ hashFiles('.pre-commit-config.yaml') }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          os="$(. /etc/os-release && printf '%s-%s' "${ID}" "${VERSION_ID}")"
          version="$(pre-commit --version | awk '{print $2}')"
          key="pre-commit-4|${os}|${version}|${pythonLocation}|${CONFIG_HASH}"
          echo "Cache key: ${key}"
          echo "key=${key}" >> "${GITHUB_OUTPUT}"

      # Restore and save are separate steps rather than one `actions/cache`
      # step whose post step saves after the job (#472). `pre-commit run`
      # executes third-party hook code, which can rewrite
      # `~/.cache/pre-commit`; a combined step would then save the modified
      # directory. Run on the default branch, that save lands in the
      # default-branch cache scope, which every branch of the consumer
      # restores from. Hence:
      #
      # - the save runs only for `pull_request` events, whose cache scope is
      #   `refs/pull/N/merge` and is readable by that pull request alone. A
      #   default-branch run, a push to any other branch, a merge-queue run
      #   and `pull_request_target` (which runs in the base branch's scope)
      #   restore at most and never save;
      # - the save runs right after `install-hooks` and before
      #   `pre-commit run`, so hook execution can no longer reach the saved
      #   directory. Install-time code of the hook repositories (pip build
      #   backends, npm scripts) still runs before it, but only within the
      #   pull request's own scope.
      #
      # Cost: nothing is saved into the default-branch scope any more, so
      # default-branch runs and the first run of each pull request install
      # cold; the second run of a pull request restores. A consumer that calls
      # this workflow only on `push` never caches.
      #
      # Accepted residual risk: hook code can read `ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN` from
      # runner memory (passwordless sudo) and write any cache key in the run's
      # own scope, the default branch's on a default-branch run. Splitting the
      # steps cannot close that path; only running the hooks isolated from the
      # runner context can.
      - name: Restore pre-commit hook environments
        id: cache-restore
        uses: actions/cache/restore@0057852bfaa89a56745cba8c7296529d2fc39830 # v4.3.0
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pre-commit
          key: ${{ steps.cache-key.outputs.key }}

      - name: Install hook environments
        # Every hook environment -- the pip/npm/... install of each third-party
        # hook repository -- is built here, as are the cache restore and the
        # pip install above, all before any Docker Hub credential exists on the
        # runner. The login below writes `~/.docker/config.json` only for
        # `pre-commit run`, which needs it because `language: docker_image`
        # hooks pull lazily through `docker run`. Accepted trade-off: hooks with
        # `language: docker` build their image in this step, so their
        # base-image pulls stay anonymous and count against the shared per-IP
        # rate limit. Unlike `pre-commit run`, which installs only the hooks of
        # the stage it runs, `install-hooks` builds the environments of every
        # stage -- `manual` and `commit-msg` hooks included -- so a consumer
        # whose non-default-stage hook cannot be installed on this runner fails
        # here, although `pre-commit run` would never execute that hook.
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          pre-commit install-hooks

      - name: Save pre-commit hook environments
        # See the comment above `Restore pre-commit hook environments`. Only on
        # a miss: a cache entry is immutable, so saving over a hit would only
        # emit a "cache already exists" warning.
        if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && steps.cache-restore.outputs.cache-hit != 'true' }}
        uses: actions/cache/save@0057852bfaa89a56745cba8c7296529d2fc39830 # v4.3.0
        with:
          path: ~/.cache/pre-commit
          key: ${{ steps.cache-key.outputs.key }}

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        id: dockerhub-login
        # Skipped, not failed, when the caller supplies nothing. An anonymous
        # pull is the status quo, and a reusable workflow that started demanding
        # a new secret would break every consumer on its next call.
        if: ${{ inputs.dockerhub-username != '' }}
        # continue-on-error, unlike the App-token step in
        # `reusable-branch-protection-audit.yaml`, where a degraded token makes
        # every repository look unprotected and a wrong answer beats no answer.
        # Here the fallback is not degraded, it is the previous behaviour: an
        # expired token, a token withheld from a fork's pull request, or a
        # username set without one all land back on anonymous pulls. Hard-failing
        # instead would redden the required lane on every pull request in the
        # consuming repository -- strictly worse than the rate limit this step
        # exists to avoid. The next step says out loud which mode was used.
        continue-on-error: true
        uses: docker/login-action@c94ce9fb468520275223c153574b00df6fe4bcc9 # v3.7.0
        with:
          username: ${{ inputs.dockerhub-username }}
          password: ${{ secrets.dockerhub-token }}

      - name: Report the registry mode this run will use
        # Always runs, including after a failed login, so the log states the
        # mode rather than leaving it to be inferred from a step's colour.
        env:
          LOGIN_OUTCOME: ${{ steps.dockerhub-login.outcome }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          case "${LOGIN_OUTCOME}" in
            success)
              echo "Docker Hub: authenticated pulls (per-account rate limit)."
              ;;
            skipped)
              echo "Docker Hub: anonymous pulls (per-IP rate limit shared with" \
                   "other runners). Set the 'dockerhub-username' input and the" \
                   "'dockerhub-token' secret to authenticate."
              ;;
            *)
              echo "::warning title=Docker Hub login failed::Continuing with" \
                   "anonymous pulls, which are rate limited per source IP." \
                   "Check the 'dockerhub-username' input and the" \
                   "'dockerhub-token' secret of the calling workflow."
              ;;
          esac

      - name: Run pre-commit
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          pre-commit run --show-diff-on-failure --color=always --all-files
